title: The sibling axis: finding a row by what it says

blocks.text:
# Week 2 - Day 4 - TypeScript

Day 4.2's Playwright code — creating, finding, updating, and deleting an employee — uses
only TypeScript you already have. This lesson is a pointer, not a primer.

> **This day introduces no new TypeScript**, so there is no primer to work through. Go
> straight to [Day 4.2](/learn/w2/d4/p2).

| | |
|---|---|
| **What *is* new** | one locator technique, the sibling axis — and a new app, because it needs a real table |
| **Then go to** | [Day 4.2](/learn/w2/d4/p2) |

## What today's code leans on

| Concept | Status | Where it was taught |
|---|---|---|
| `const`, dynamic typing | already covered | [Week 2, Day 2.1](/learn/w2/d2/p1) |
| `Math.random()` for a unique value | already covered | [Week 2, Day 3.1](/learn/w2/d3/p1) |
| XPath vs CSS, first real assertions | already covered | [Week 2, Day 2.2](/learn/w2/d2/p2) |
| `async` functions, arrow functions | already covered | [Week 1, Day 5.1](/learn/w1/d5/p1) |
| "structure around it" = a function, not a class | already covered | [Week 2, Day 1.3](/learn/w2/d1/p3) |

Nothing below is new syntax — [Day 4.2](/learn/w2/d4/p2) spends its time on one new
*locator* technique (the sibling axis), not the language. It just happens to run
against a new app, because that technique needs a real multi-row table to show off —
more on that in Day 4.2's first cell.
Day 4 switches to OrangeHRM's demo HR system instead of the registration form used all week. Why?

options: Because the registration form's locators had started to break
Because today's technique finds one row among many that look alike, and none of the earlier apps has a real multi-row table
Because the sibling axis only works on applications built with tables
checkpoint.explanation: The app changed to fit the technique, not the other way round. It is also a shared public sandbox, which is why every employee the lesson creates gets deleted before the lesson ends.

blocks.text: Today's code uses `const`, `Math.random()`, XPath and `async`, all from earlier this week. If any row in the table above was a surprise, follow its link before starting [Day 4.2](/learn/w2/d4/p2).

## What's next

[Day 4.2 — The sibling axis](/learn/w2/d4/p2) puts everything above to work finding a table
row by what it says, not where it sits.

parts.title: The sibling axis: finding a row by what it says

blocks.text:
# Week 2 - Day 4 - Fundamentals - The sibling axis: finding a row by what it says

By the end of this lesson you will have created a real employee on a live HR system,
found its row by the name you gave it (not by counting columns), updated it, verified
the change for real, and deleted it — cleaning up after yourself the whole way.

| | |
|---|---|
| **You'll use** | `parent::` · `following-sibling::` · `[last()]` · `contains()` |
| **On** | OrangeHRM's demo HR system — a **shared public sandbox**, so everything created here is deleted again |
| **Assumes** | [XPath syntax](/learn/w2/d2/p2) · [Math.random() for unique data](/learn/w2/d3/p1) |
| **The idea worth keeping** | anchor on text you know, then walk sideways — never count columns |

> **Try it here**, with one real spec at the end.

## A new app, on purpose

Every locator so far worked on a single form. Today's technique — finding one row among
many that all look alike — needs an actual table, which none of this course's apps so
far have. **OrangeHRM's demo HR system** does, and it's a real, public, shared QA-practice
app (the same idea as `demoqa.com`, used from [week7](/learn/w7/d1/p1) onward).

| | |
|---|---|
| App | `opensource-demo.orangehrmlive.com` |
| Login | `Admin` / `admin123` |
| Screens used | Add Employee, Employee List |

**It's shared with everyone using this demo right now.** Every employee this lesson
creates gets deleted before the lesson ends — the same rule week7 follows for
`demoqa.com`.

## The problem: which column is "Actions"?

A table row usually looks like this once rendered:

```
| Id | First Name | Last Name | Job Title | Status | Sub Unit | Supervisor | Actions |
```

You could count to column 8 and write `.nth(7)` — until a column gets added, hidden per
screen size, or reordered, and every locator built that way breaks at once.

| Approach | What it commits to |
|---|---|
| Guess the column index (`.nth(7)`) | Wherever "Actions" happens to sit today |
| Anchor on text you already know (a name you just typed), then walk **sideways** to the last cell in that same row | The row itself — position never enters into it |

The second one is the **sibling axis**: find something you know for certain, then step to
its neighbours rather than re-finding your way from the top of the page.

## Example 1 — create an employee

**Objective:** add a real employee with a name unique enough to find again later.

Line by line:

| Line | What it does |
|---|---|
| `Math.floor(Math.random() * 100000)` | Day 3.1's technique — a value unlikely to collide with anyone else on this shared demo |
| `page.getByRole("button", { name: "Save" })` | Same role-based locator you've used since Day 1 — new app, same idea |
| `p.oxd-text--toast-message` | OrangeHRM's toast element — probed live before writing this, one clean match |

**Expected result:** `toast: Successfully Saved`, then the URL ends in
`viewPersonalDetails/empNumber/<some id>` — the app navigates you straight to the new
employee's record. **Keep `lastName` and `idPart` around — every cell below builds on
this same employee.**

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

variation.prompt: Same steps, your own marker: use a different first name as well as the generated last name, and log the `empNumber` out of the URL the app redirects you to. Keep `lastName` and `idPart` in scope — every cell below needs them, and Example 4 is what deletes this employee again.

blocks.text:
## Example 2 — finding the row you just made

**Objective:** search the employee list, then reach the row's Actions cell by anchoring on
the last name — not by guessing a column.

| Piece of the XPath | Why it's there |
|---|---|
| `//div[text()='${lastName}']` | the cell holding exactly the name you typed |
| `/parent::div` | **the gotcha** — the text sits in an inner wrapper div with no siblings of its own; the real table-cell divs are one level up |
| `/following-sibling::div[last()]` | walk sideways to the **last** cell in that row, whatever column it's in — this is Actions, no matter how many cells sit in between |

`[last()]` is the whole trick: it reaches the last cell in the row regardless of how many
cells sit in between, so it never needs to know the exact count — the same idea as
reaching for "the last one" instead of "the fourth one" whenever a list's length isn't
fixed.

**Expected result:** `rows found: 1`, `buttons in actions cell: 2`, then the URL changes
to `viewPersonalDetails/...` — you clicked the pencil (edit) icon. **Verified live: the
pencil is always the first button in that cell, the trash the second** — `.first()` and
`.last()` below aren't a guess.

**Challenge:** what happens to the XPath if you search `contains(text(), ...)` instead of
an exact match? (You'll need exactly this for Example 4.)

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

variation.prompt: Same row, one axis at a time: print the match count for each stage of the XPath separately — `//div[text()='...']` on its own, then with `/parent::div` appended, then with `/following-sibling::div[last()]`. Watching where the number changes shows you the `parent::div` trap directly, instead of taking it on trust.

blocks.text:
## Example 3 — update it, and verify for real

**Objective:** change the last name, and prove the change landed by reloading the record —
not by trusting the toast.

**Expected result:** `value after reload: Verify<idPart>Updated`, usually on the first
attempt. If you see a retry line above it, that's the demo being slow to save — not
your code; the loop exists precisely so this cell tells the truth either way.

**Why reload, not re-search?** The Employee List's search index can lag a rename by more
than this app's own toast implies. Reloading the record itself reads the ground truth
directly, the same "assert the consequence, don't trust the response" habit from
[week7](/learn/w7/d4/p2).

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

variation.prompt: Same verification, pointed the other way: once the reload has confirmed the new last name, go back to the Employee List and search for the OLD one. Print the row count. Whether you get 0 or 1 tells you how far behind the list's search index is right now — which is exactly why Example 4 anchors on the random id instead of either name.

blocks.text:
## Example 4 — delete it, and prove it's gone

**Objective:** re-find the row and delete it — anchoring on `contains()`, not an exact
match, because the list may still be showing the *old* last name.

**Expected result:** `delete toast: Successfully Deleted`, then `rows found after
delete: 0` — a negative assertion, not just "the toast said so". The dialog text
(`"Are you sure you want to continue?"`) and both its button names were confirmed live
before writing this.

**Challenge:** re-run Examples 1–4 back to back a second time. Nothing should be left
behind either time — that's the whole point of pairing every create with a delete.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

variation.prompt: Same cleanup, one more proof: after the delete, assert that the "No Records Found" message is actually visible, not only that the row count is 0. Two ways of saying the same thing — and an empty table with no message would quietly pass the first check while failing the second.

blocks.text:
## Doing it for real, in a spec file

The cell below writes everything above as one real test, hardened against the two
measured quirks: a click that silently does nothing (an overlay steals it for a moment),
and the update-toast timing.

> ▶ **Run it yourself too:** `npx playwright test week2/generated/day4-employee-crud.spec.ts`

**Expected result:** `1 passed`, typically in 30–60 seconds — a real create, find,
update-with-retry, and delete against a live public system. Verified green three runs in
a row while writing this lesson.

## Best practices

- Anchor on text you just created or already know — never a column position.
- `parent::div` before `following-sibling` — the text's immediate parent is a wrapper,
  not the cell.
- Prefer `contains()` over an exact match once you can't be sure the visible text hasn't
  changed underneath you.
- Verify a write by reading the record back, not by trusting a success toast.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | What you see | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `following-sibling::div[1]` (guessing an offset) | works today, breaks the moment a column is added | `[last()]` — Actions is always last, regardless of count |
| Anchoring straight off the text node | 0 matches | go `parent::div` first |
| Trusting "Successfully Updated" alone | the list search for the new name comes back empty | reload the record and read the field back |
| Two "Save" buttons, wrong one clicked with a plain `getByRole` | `.first()` needed, or the search finds the correct one only sometimes | `.first()` and verify it's the form's own button |
The Actions cell is currently the 8th column. Why is `following-sibling::div[last()]` better than `.nth(7)`?

options: It is faster, because XPath does not have to count the cells
It asks for the last cell in the row whatever the column count is, so adding or reordering a column cannot break it
`.nth()` does not work on table rows in Playwright
checkpoint.explanation: `.nth(7)` commits to wherever Actions happens to sit today — one added, hidden or reordered column and every locator built that way breaks at once. `[last()]` commits only to "the last cell in this row", which stays true. Same instinct as reaching for "the last one" instead of "the fourth one" whenever the length is not fixed.

blocks.text: Without the `parent::div` step, `//div[text()='Verify12345']/following-sibling::div[last()]` returns how many matches?

options: 1 — it is the same row either way
0 — the text sits in an inner wrapper div that has no siblings; the real cells are one level up
2 — it matches the cell and the row
checkpoint.explanation: This is the trap the lesson calls out by name. The element holding the text is a wrapper inside the cell, and it has no siblings at all, so stepping sideways from it finds nothing. `/parent::div` first gets you to the real table cell, which does have siblings.

blocks.text: The app shows "Successfully Updated". What does the lesson do before believing the rename landed?

options: Waits for the toast to disappear, then continues
Reloads the record and reads the field back, retrying the save if it does not match
Re-searches the Employee List for the new name
checkpoint.explanation: Measured on this live demo, the toast can fire a beat before the save actually lands. Reloading the record reads ground truth. Re-searching the list is worse than useless here — its search index can lag a rename by even longer, which is why Example 4 anchors on the random id instead of either name.

blocks.text:
- **Anchor on text you know, then walk sideways.** Position is the one thing about a table you can rely on changing.
- `/parent::div` before `following-sibling::` — the text's immediate parent is a wrapper, not the cell.
- `[last()]` over a guessed offset: it survives a column being added.
- `contains()` once you cannot be certain the visible text has not changed underneath you — and anchor on the part that cannot change, like the random id.
- **Verify a write by reading the record back**, not by trusting a success toast.
- On a shared sandbox, every create is paired with a delete. Prove the delete with a count of 0, not with the toast.

## What's next

[Day 4.3](/learn/w2/d4/p3) takes this exact code and gives it a small amount of structure.

parts.title: The sibling axis, wrapped for reuse

blocks.text:
# Week 2 - Day 4 - Implementation - The sibling axis, wrapped for reuse

By the end of this lesson you will have pulled Day 4.2's create/find/delete steps out
of one long cell and into three functions any test can call.

> **No new API here on purpose.** Everything below is something you already ran in
> [Day 4.2](/learn/w2/d4/p2). The only new thing is the structure around it.

| | |
|---|---|
| **The API** | every line ran in [Day 4.2](/learn/w2/d4/p2) |
| **What changes** | create, find and delete each become a function; the long cell becomes three calls |
| **The design decision** | `findRow` locates and returns — it never clicks. The caller decides what happens next. |

## The problem with what we wrote yesterday

Every test that needs to create, find, or delete an employee has to repeat the same
sibling-axis XPath and the same button clicks. Three uses today, thirty in a real suite —
and if the app's markup shifts, that is thirty edits, not one.

## Same code, with structure around it

| In Day 4.2 you wrote | Here it becomes | Why |
|---|---|---|
| the create steps inline in a cell | `await addEmployee(page, lastName)` | one place to change if the Add Employee form changes |
| the sibling-axis XPath rebuilt each time | `await findRow(page, term)` | the pattern lives in one place, not re-derived per test |
| the trash-click-then-confirm steps inline | `await deleteEmployee(page, term)` | reusable cleanup, same as `findRow` underneath |

**This is still a function, not a page object.** A real page object — a `class` that
never asserts — is [coming formally in week 3](/learn/w3/d3/p1), the same as Day
1.3, Day 2.3, and Day 3.3 already told you. Today's version reaches for the same tool
those days did: three plain functions.

### Why it is shaped this way

| Choice | Reason |
|---|---|
| `findRow` returns a `Locator`, doesn't click anything | the caller decides whether that's a pencil click, a trash click, or just a count — one function, several uses |
| `term: string`, not `lastName: string`, in `findRow`/`deleteEmployee` | Day 4.2 showed the same anchor is sometimes the full name, sometimes just the id — the parameter name says so |
| No `expect()` anywhere in this file | these functions act and locate; the *test* decides what should be true |
| Update has no function of its own yet | it's still two field edits and a click in the test — a natural next problem, in [Day 4.4](/learn/w2/d4/p4) |

## Using it

**Objective:** create an employee, edit it via the row `findRow` returns, then delete it —
using only the three functions above.

**Expected result:** `created: Verify<idPart>`, `updated to: Verify<idPart>Updated`,
`deleted`, then `rows after delete: 0`. Same outcome as Day 4.2 — the create, update, and
delete steps just moved into functions the test calls by name.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

variation.prompt: Same three helpers, a different caller: write a short flow that creates an employee, uses `findRow` only to COUNT the buttons in its actions cell, and then deletes it — never clicking the pencil at all. That is the whole reason `findRow` hands back a locator instead of doing the click for you.

blocks.text:
## Doing it for real, in a spec file

Same helpers, imported from a real `.spec.ts` this time — `expect()` lives in the test,
never inside `employee-list-helpers.ts`.

> ▶ **Run it yourself too:** `npx playwright test week2/generated/day4-reuse.spec.ts`

**Expected result:** `1 passed`. Verified green twice while writing this lesson.

## What a reviewer would look for

- `findRow` returns a locator and clicks nothing — the caller decides what to do with it.
- Nothing inside `employee-list-helpers.ts` calls `expect()`.
- The random id, not a hardcoded name, is what makes this test safe to run twice in a row.
`findRow` returns a `Locator` and clicks nothing. What does that buy?

options: One function serves every use — a pencil click, a trash click, or just counting the buttons
It makes the function synchronous, so callers need no `await`
It lets Playwright cache the row between tests
checkpoint.explanation: A `findRow` that clicked the pencil itself would need a sibling function for the trash, and a third for counting. Returning the locator keeps the sideways-walk in one place and leaves the decision to the caller — which is why `deleteEmployee` can be built on top of it.

blocks.text: There is not one `expect()` in `employee-list-helpers.ts`. Why not?

options: Because `expect()` cannot be called outside a `.spec.ts` file
Because these functions act and locate — the test is what decides what should be true
Because the helpers run before the test does, when no assertions are allowed yet
checkpoint.explanation: Same separation as [Day 2.3](/learn/w2/d2/p3), from the other side: there the assertion helper was allowed to assert because checking was its whole job. These functions act, so they do not. A helper that both acts and asserts leaves a caller unable to use it for either job alone.

blocks.text:
- Three uses today is thirty in a real suite — and a markup change is then thirty edits.
- A locator function should hand back the locator, not decide what to do with it.
- Name the parameter for what it really is: `term`, not `lastName`, because sometimes the anchor is just the id.
- Helpers act and locate; tests assert. Keep the two on opposite sides of the file boundary.
- The random id, not a fixed name, is what makes any of this safe to run twice in a row.

## What's next

[Day 4.4](/learn/w2/d4/p4) — your turn, with no worked examples to lean on.

# Week 2 - Day 4 - Practice - The sibling axis

Three problems, getting harder. There is no answer key — that is deliberate. Every
employee you create in these problems is on a real, shared, public system: **delete it
before you move on**, using the same sibling-axis pattern from Day 4.2.

Start in a fresh cell in this lesson. When a problem asks for a spec file, write it
into `week2/generated/` and run it with `npx playwright test`.

> Struggling for more than about twenty minutes on one problem means the gap is in
> [Day 4.1](/learn/w2/d4/p1) or [Day 4.2](/learn/w2/d4/p2), not in your ability.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Three problems** | on a live, shared HR system |
| **Pulls on** | [Day 4.2](/learn/w2/d4/p2) for the axes · [Day 4.3](/learn/w2/d4/p3) for the helper shape |
| **Non-negotiable** | anything you create, you delete — someone else is using this demo right now |

## When you are done

Search the Employee List one more time for every name you used above. If anything still
shows up, delete it now — this app is shared with everyone else using this course.

problems.statement:
**What to build.** Create an employee with a different unique last name than the ones
used in Day 4.2 (still `"Verify" + a random number` is fine — just a fresh call to
`Math.random()`). Find its row with the sibling axis, then delete it.

**Where.** A cell in this lesson.

**How you will know it worked.** The "Successfully Saved" toast, then the "Successfully
Deleted" toast, then a re-search for that name comes back with 0 rows.

> **Hint** — this is Day 4.2's Example 1 and Example 4, back to back, with no update
> step in between.

**What to build.** Create one employee, then update its last name **twice** — once to a
value with "Round1" appended, then again to a value with "Round2" appended — verifying
each change actually persisted (reload and check, the way Day 4.2's Example 3 did)
before moving on to the next. Delete it at the end.

**Where.** A cell here, or a spec in `week2/generated/` if you want the real `expect()`.

**How you will know it worked.** Two separate "value after reload" checks, each matching
the name you just set — not the name from the previous round.

**What to build.** Extend `week2/generated/employee-list-helpers.ts` (from
[Day 4.3](/learn/w2/d4/p3)) with a fourth function:

```ts
export async function updateLastName(page: Page, oldLastName: string, newLastName: string): Promise<void>
```

It should find the row for `oldLastName`, click the pencil, fill in `newLastName`, save,
and reload to confirm — the same retry pattern Day 4.2 and 4.3 already used, just moved
inside the function this time. Then write a test in `week2/generated/` that creates an
employee, calls `updateLastName`, and deletes it — using **only** the four functions, no
raw locators in the test itself.

**Where.** A spec in `week2/generated/`.

**How you will know it worked.** The test passes, and nothing in it references
`page.locator(...)` or an XPath directly — only calls to the helper functions.
